title: Following the grain: wood, tools and the discipline of carving
deck: Woodcarving joins botanical material to learned hand skills: the grain guides each cut, while chisels, mallets and repeated patterns carry knowledge between makers.
geography_label: Konjic, Bosnia and Herzegovina; comparative workshop image from Uzbekistan

sources.title: Konjic woodcarving — traditional craftsmanship in Bosnia and Herzegovina
Sculpture techniques: carving wood and understanding material direction

sections.heading: The material answers each cut
sections.text: Wood is anisotropic: it does not behave identically in every direction. A carver reads grain, knots and density before choosing the angle and depth of a cut, adapting a planned form to the particular piece in hand.

sections.heading: Chisel, gouge and mallet
sections.text: Carving tools remove wood in controlled increments. Straight chisels define planes and edges, curved gouges open hollows and channels, and a mallet supplies measured force while the maker directs the edge.

sections.heading: A documented tradition in Konjic
sections.text: UNESCO describes Konjic woodcarving as a living craft used for furniture, interiors and smaller decorative objects. Recognisable patterns are drawn and cut, while knowledge passes through workshops and apprenticeships.

sections.heading: Repetition builds judgement
sections.text: A pattern can be transferred, but the cut is never fully automatic. Tool sharpness, hand position and the changing grain require continuous judgement. Apprentices learn motifs and when to stop, turn or change tools.

sections.heading: Durability and repair
sections.text: Wooden objects move as humidity changes and can split along grain or joints. Conservation attends to environment, coatings and prior repairs; aggressive refinishing may remove tool marks and evidence of manufacture.

sections.heading: One image is not one tradition
sections.text: The cover documents a woodcarver in Uzbekistan and is a comparative workshop image, not Konjic practice. Cultural claims remain tied to UNESCO’s named Bosnian tradition rather than generalized across regions.
